title: Exploring protein conformations beyond fixed-end loops
summary: A modular C++/Python sampler for protein loops, fragments, and intrinsically disordered regions, paired with explicit all-atom validation.
question: How can a loop-closure method explore protein segments whose endpoints are free to move?
context: Fixed-end loop closure addresses an important but constrained sampling problem. Exploring fragments and disordered regions requires one or both endpoints to move while maintaining feasible local backbone geometry.
My work extends the geometric sampling machinery and separates conformational exploration from downstream evaluation of structural quality.
role: Extended and optimized the C++ sampler and built its all-atom validation workflow.

steps.title: Extend the sampler
steps.text: Support fixed or independently released endpoints, multiple loops, and rigid secondary-structure motion.

steps.title: Propose conformations
steps.text: Combine geometric endpoint moves with residue-specific Ramachandran priors and spatial-hash clash detection.

steps.title: Validate structures
steps.text: Reconstruct side chains, minimize with OpenMM, and assess conformational quality and ensemble diversity.

contributions: Implemented released-anchor SE(3) proposals and multiple sampling frames.
Engineered spatial-hash collision detection and dense/sparse memory backends.
Integrated AttnPacker, OpenMM, and PhiSiCal-Checkup in a reproducible validation workflow.
Resolved stability and zero-output failure modes in the sampling software.
validation: Controlled comparisons with tested generative samplers showed broader exploration on the evaluated systems. This is a system-specific observation, not a claim of general superiority.
Ongoing work: no unpublished manuscript figures, raw benchmark data, or unfinished software releases are distributed here.

title: From molecular structure to scalable self-assembly simulation
summary: Automated structure-to-simulation workflows and a parallel particle-based reaction-diffusion engine, with numerical validation built in.
question: How do we turn a molecular structure into a usable model—and simulate it at larger scales without losing numerical correctness?
context: Preparing a structure-resolved reaction-diffusion model requires identifying interfaces, defining coarse-grained geometry, and enumerating reactions. ioNERDSS connects those steps in a Python workflow.

Large particle-based simulations introduce an additional challenge: reactions and assemblies must remain consistent across processor boundaries. NERDSS-MPI addresses this through spatial domain decomposition and distributed communication.
role: Co-developed ioNERDSS and led MPI design, implementation, validation, and benchmarking for NERDSS.

steps.title: Build the model
steps.text: Convert PDB/mmCIF structures into coarse-grained models using KD-tree interface detection, reaction generation, and sequence alignment.

steps.title: Distribute the work
steps.text: Partition space across MPI processes and communicate particle, reaction, and assembly information across domain boundaries.

steps.title: Verify the result
steps.text: Compare diffusion, reactions, assembly, dissociation, and restart behavior against analytical theory and serial simulations.

contributions: Implemented C++/MPI spatial domain decomposition and distributed communication.
Validated distributed algorithms across seven benchmark models spanning diffusion, membrane reactions, and clathrin assembly.
Developed automated structure processing and reaction-model construction, including ML-assisted affinity initialization.
Released Python simulation, restart, analysis, and visualization workflows with tests, packaging, and documentation.
validation: Approximately 90× speedup on 96 CPUs for a 20,000-particle benchmark; this is a measured workload-specific result, not a universal scaling guarantee.
Structure-processing workflows benchmarked on 44,000+ structures and assemblies ranging from 3 to 720 subunits.
Distributed results were checked against analytical theory and serial simulation across seven benchmark models.

title: One specification. Consistent scientific applications.
summary: A Python framework that generates PyMOL, VMD, and web applications from a reusable application specification.
question: How can scientific tools reach multiple user-interface platforms without maintaining a separate implementation for every tool?
context: Building a separate GUI for every application-platform pair duplicates work and makes synchronized changes difficult. AutoCLIP treats an application description as a reusable specification.
Platform adapters generate interfaces while keeping application state, execution logic, post-analysis, and molecular visualization modular.
role: Designed the framework architecture and implemented specification validation and platform generators.

steps.title: Describe the application
steps.text: Combine interface layout, command-line metadata, and exposed analysis parameters.

steps.title: Validate the specification
steps.text: Convert the description into a platform-independent JSON representation and validate its structure.

steps.title: Generate and deploy
steps.text: Use reusable adapters to create applications for PyMOL, VMD, and the web.

contributions: Architected a specification-driven framework with Model–View–Presenter separation.
Implemented JSON Schema validation, Qt interface parsing, and platform-specific generators.
Built cross-platform tests and CI/CD for Linux and Intel/Apple Silicon macOS.
Added reproducible Pixi/Conda packaging and authenticated web deployment.
validation: Deployed nine structural-biology applications across PyMOL, VMD, and web environments.
The architecture uses one specification per application and reusable platform adapters rather than independent implementations for every application-platform pair.

title: Linking molecular interactions to assembly and remodeling
summary: Mechanistic models of clathrin and HIV lattices that connect molecular interactions to experimentally observed assembly behavior.
question: What determines whether a molecular assembly stabilizes, disassembles, or remodels?
context: Molecular structures alone do not describe how assemblies emerge over time. My models combine structural information with stochastic simulation, kinetic measurements, and interaction constraints.
The goal is to connect microscopic interaction rules to experimentally interpretable assembly behavior rather than reproduce a single structural snapshot.
role: Designed and analyzed clathrin and HIV-1 models and contributed quantitative modeling to collaborative studies.

steps.title: Define molecular interactions
steps.text: Build structure-resolved models with explicit interaction affinities, concentrations, and membrane geometry.

steps.title: Simulate assembly dynamics
steps.text: Study association, dissociation, nucleation, and remodeling using stochastic reaction-diffusion models.

steps.title: Connect to experiments
steps.text: Compare kinetics and timescales with experiments and identify mechanistic explanations.

contributions: Modeled clathrin self-assembly and reproduced experimental kinetics.
Explained why adaptor-poor clathrin lattices fail to stabilize.
Identified a binding-affinity range compatible with both HIV Gag/Gag-Pol lattice stability and remodeling.
Contributed quantitative modeling to collaborative work on dynamin recruitment and membrane nanoclusters.
validation: First-author clathrin work published in PLOS Computational Biology (2022).
First-author HIV lattice work published in eLife (2023), with remodeling on experimentally observed viral-maturation timescales.
Collaborative dynamin work published in Nature Communications (2024).
